safetyNote: Coprinus comatus is listed as edible when very young, fresh and correctly identified, while the gills and flesh are still white. It deteriorates rapidly: do not eat specimens with pink, black or liquefying gills, and prepare verified young specimens promptly and thoroughly. Sources disagree about alcohol-related risk: a review reports no established coprine in this species, while Chinese poisoning surveillance associates it with alcohol-related illness. Avoid alcohol with wild inkcaps and seek poison-centre advice after symptoms.

sections.title: Young fruit body
sections.text: The shaggy inkcap begins with a tall, narrow, white cylindrical to elongated bell-shaped cap, commonly 5–15 cm high and up to about 6 cm across. Whitish, upturned shaggy fibres and scales cover its surface, while a small smooth tip is tan to pale brown. The white stem is slender, brittle and hollow, sometimes slightly wider at the base. A thin movable ring may be present and can slide down or disappear with age.

sections.title: Gills and deliquescence
sections.text: The densely packed gills are initially white, becoming pink and then black. The outer cap edge and gills progressively digest themselves into a black liquid, curling upward as the process moves toward the centre. At the end a small dark disc may remain on the stem. The spore deposit is black. These stages are part of normal maturation, but only young white-gilled specimens are treated as food.

sections.title: Ecology and season
sections.text: A saprobic species of nutrient-rich ground, lawns, gardens, pathsides, grassy verges and open woodland. It often grows in groups, lines or arcs after rain. In much of Europe it fruits from spring into late autumn, especially in summer and autumn. Avoid collecting from potentially contaminated sites such as busy roadsides.

sections.title: Confusion and alcohol
sections.text: Coprinopsis atramentaria, the common inkcap, has a smooth grey-brown cap rather than a tall white shaggy one and can trigger a coprine–alcohol reaction. Other inkcaps may look similar when young, including C. picacea, which develops white patches on a darker cap. A scientific review reports no established coprine in C. comatus, but a Chinese surveillance study reports poisoning incidents involving this species and alcohol, without toxin measurement of every specimen. This discrepancy merits caution rather than a blanket assurance.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The white-background plate compares a complete fresh white shaggy specimen with a later fruit body showing pink and black, liquefying cap margins. A longitudinal cut reveals the hollow stem and young gills; a separate underside view shows the early change at the gill edges.
